newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Hanbo scandal still haunts S.Korea economy.
newsitem.headline: Hanbo scandal still haunts S.Korea economy.

text.p: The troubles of South Korea's Kia Group show how the Hanbo loans-for-kickbacks scandal continues to reverberate through the economy, bankers and analysts said on Wednesday.

Companies that by all rational accounts are sound now are experiencing cash-flow problems as jittery lenders keep a tight hold on credit in the aftermath of the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co in January under $5.6 billion of debt.
Merchant banks, which have been portrayed as culprits in a series of post-Hanbo corporate failures, said their nervousness was natural because they extend credit with little or no collateral.
"We have become very sensitive about our clients' financial conditions since Hanbo. Even a rumour can scare us," said Park Ji-kwang, a finance manager at Hansol Merchant Bank.
That appears to be what happened to the eighth-ranked Kia Group.

Bankers said the non-banking institutions moved quickly to reduce their exposure to Kia after a report leaked by Samsung Motors alleged managerial conflicts within Kia group flagship Kia Motors Corp and hinted of a takeover.
Kia strongly denied the allegations and filed a complaint against Samsung.
Analysts said merchant banks held about half of the Kia Group's estimated debts of 10 trillion won ($11.27 billion).
"But we don't want the car maker to go bankrupt because that means losing all of our credits to the company," Park said.
Merchant bank officials complained about a growing reluctance among banks to ease the burden shouldered by secondary lenders.
They are particularly bitter about a bank rescue committee that acts to save certain companies by keeping their credit lines open regardless of the impact on secondary lenders.

"As long as banks, investment trusts and pension funds roll over commercial paper (CP) they bought from us, all will be fine. But once trouble surfaces, they don't want to hold it," a spokesman for the Merchant Banks' Association of Korea said.
Bankers, however, said merchant banks had stopped guaranteeing CP.
"Who will want to keep paper not guaranteed by anyone?" said Na Byung-rok, spokesman at the Korea First Bank, Kia's main creditor.
Lee Hahn-koo, president of Daewoo Research Institute, said: "It is a matter of trust. Trust should come from lenders' reasonable assessments about credit ratings of CP issuers."
Analysts said the future of Kia depended on how well the conglomerate was able to convince its lenders of its soundness.
"The group is at a crossroads. It has to come up with more tangible measures, such as a plan to resolve chronic labour problems and improve management leadership," Daewoo's Lee said.

Kia Motors has been viewed as an easy takeover target because of the company's thinly spread shareholdings. Kia's largest shareholder, Ford Motor Co, holds 16.91 percent with no management rights. Kia employees hold 13.81 percent.
Group spokesman Ahn Suk-woo said Kia planned to cut its payroll, merge affiliates and sell idle assets.
On Tuesday, the group said Asia Motors, the group's commercial vehicle arm, would raise about 520 billion won by moving its plant to a cheaper site two to three years ahead of schedule.
The group also said it would sell some 795 billion won worth of idle assets.
On Wednesday, state-run Korea Development Bank provided 30 billion won in emergency loans to the group's Kia Steel.
